view: Establish the prescribed prayers by performing their required acts fully, including bowing and prostration.
Establishing prayer also means performing it regularly and without interruption, or performing it well at its prescribed times.
The verse specifies prayer periods in general; the Prophet's teaching and practice explain their exact times, form, units, conditions, and other details.
The command emphasizes the five obligatory prayers, whose times are understood here by many commentators.
Prayer should fill one's day and night through obligatory and voluntary worship and constant remembrance, while allowing work, sleep, and other human needs.
Ibn al-Arabi rejects making every hour a prayer time: the command concerns obligations, while voluntary devotions have bounded times and alternate with other acts.
Prayer follows steadfastness as the highest worship and the strongest aid to uprightness after faith, a refuge in hardship and especially potent against the weakness behind minor sins.
The Prophet receives positive commands directly while prohibitions address the community; this dignifies him and implies that the prohibited transgression is possible among them.
The prayer command echoes the command to Moses to establish prayer for God's remembrance in 20:14.
Prayer's placement after the call to steadfastness connects it with the surrounding commands and the remedy for distress.
The two day ends denote Fajr at the first end and Maghrib at the second.
note: Al-Tabari argues that opposite boundaries require Maghrib; critics object that sunset belongs to night.

view: The two day ends denote Fajr and Asr.
note: Some include Zuhr in the latter end; this view names Asr alone.

view: The first end is Fajr; the latter end includes Zuhr and Asr.
note: The objection is that Zuhr occurs after midday and is not itself a day boundary.

view: The two day ends are Zuhr and Asr; Fajr is counted with Maghrib and Isha among night or adjacent prayers, sometimes explained by loud versus quiet recitation.
note: Al-Tabari rejects Zuhr as a first boundary; Elmalılı prefers the customary division into day parts.

view: Muqatil assigns Fajr and Zuhr to one end, Asr and Maghrib to the other.
One report from Mujahid identifies the ends as Fajr and Isha.
Most agree the first edge of day is Fajr, though a reported Zuhr-first view qualifies that consensus.

Dawn is a daytime boundary because fasting begins then; the opposing objection is that Maghrib is already night. Noon and Asr may be omitted because they are obvious daytime prayers or stated in 17:78.
note: The dispute turns on whether boundary means a literal part of daytime or a time adjacent to it.

view: The literal phrase is 'the two ends of the day'; day runs from dawn to sunset, and its ends are morning and evening.
Noon and afternoon can be two customary later divisions of day when dawn is treated as its root and the morning as its body.
Other verses place worship before sunrise and sunset and describe prayer at the sun's decline, clarifying the differing assignments of the day prayers.
The accusative 'two ends of day' is an adverb of time governed by 'establish'; 'end' acquires temporal force by annexation to 'day.'
note: Al-Samin considers attachment to 'prayer' as its times weaker.

view: The yāʾ of 'ṭarafay' is vocalized when followed by a silent consonant, usually with kasra in such consonant clusters.
The night approaches are Maghrib and Isha prayers.
The night approaches mean Isha alone, at a night hour or after earlier portions of night.
note: Other reports take the phrase to include Maghrib too.

view: The phrase can refer to voluntary night prayer or the earlier required night vigil.
Other assignments add witr or tahajjud to Maghrib and Isha, or join tahajjud to Isha, treating the plural as requiring additional night worship.
Al-Akhfash interprets the phrase as night prayer without specifying which prayer.
Ibn Abbas cites the verse when preferring to delay Isha.
Razi says the verse supports Abu Hanifa's preference to perform Fajr later in its period and Asr near sunset.
The Kharijites infer only two obligatory prayers, at dawn and nightfall, reading the night phrase adjectivally; Razi rejects this as contrary to consensus.
Razi argues that plural zulf requires at least three night periods, so adding witr to Maghrib and Isha makes witr obligatory for the Prophet and all people.

Elmalılı infers from a threefold night plural a possible sixth prayer, the Prophet's tahajjud or the community's witr; five prayers are certain, while witr is a practical wājib rather than an obligation of belief.
The five prayers are to be performed in congregation; the call to prayer is sunnah and congregation is wājib.
Zulaf is the plural of zulfa, denoting successive hours, stages, or portions of night, especially near its beginning or near day.
note: Thaʿlab and al-Layth specify early night; others allow any night hour. Poetry from al-Ajjaj illustrates successive intervals.

view: The root conveys nearness or approach; zulfa can mean a rank, station, or favor, and Muzdalifa is explained as a stop after Arafat or as the place where Adam approached Eve.
note: Al-Raghib also notes an ironic euphemistic sense of punishment.

view: The base plural is zulafan, with ḍamma on zay and fatḥa on lam, plural of zulfa; analyses also give the plural as zulf, zuluf, or zulafāt.
The prevalent reading has fatḥa on lam; other readers give both zay and lam ḍamma, explained as vowel harmony, a singular pattern, or a plural of zalīf.
note: The ḍamma variant changes the internal plural pattern without changing its meaning.

view: Ibn Muhaysin and Mujahid read with silent lam; this may be a shortened vocalized form or a collective singular.
Mujahid and Ibn Muhaysin are also reported to read zulfā, like qurbā, a feminine singular for a near hour, station, or rank.
The apparent syntax coordinates 'night approaches' with the two day boundaries as another time adverb; 'of the night' qualifies 'approaches.'
Another parse coordinates night approaches with 'prayer': they are night prayers by which worshippers seek nearness to God.
The good deeds here are the five prescribed prayers, which expiate sins between prayer times.
note: Al-Tabari cites recurring prophetic reports and the immediate prayer context; Ibn al-Jawzi cites majority support and a connected report.

view: Good deeds include verbal remembrance: glorifying and praising God, declaring His oneness and greatness, and in some reports declaring reliance on Him; these are also called enduring good deeds.

The wording covers good deeds generally, including prayer, remembrance, fasting, and other obligatory or voluntary obedience grounded in faith; the named deeds are examples, with the five prayers especially important.
note: Some restrict expiation to obligations; al-Alusi cites voluntary acts as expiators.

view: One interpretation identifies the good deed chiefly as repentance, which cancels the punishment of sins, including major sins.
Good deeds remove guilt, punishment, traces, or liability from earlier sins; they do not make the past acts cease to have occurred.
An alternative takes removal to mean that persistent good deeds form habits that deter future evil and lead one to abandon sin; prayer restrains indecency.
note: Al-Alusi calls this reading remote; Ibn Ashur allows both prevention and expiation.

view: Good action should follow a bad deed to erase it; a fresh good deed is especially effective against an old sin.
note: The prophetic counsel adds fear of God and good treatment of people; Abu Ubayda says even immense old sins can be overcome.

view: Evil cannot erase evil; only a truly good deed cancels sin, so illicitly obtained wealth given as charity is not accepted.
Prayer and ablution cleanse sins between prayers, illustrated by water washing dirt or dry leaves falling from a branch.
note: Some reports require careful ablution; the river simile uses five baths, and the leaf simile a shaken dry branch.

view: After sin, thorough ablution and two prayer units without distracting thoughts bring forgiveness of prior sins.
The sins erased by ordinary good deeds are minor sins; major sins require repentance, and reports condition the expiation between prayers, Fridays, and Ramadans on avoiding major sins.
One interpretation makes avoiding major sins a condition for any lesser sins to be expiated; another treats major sins as the exception, so good deeds still erase lesser sins without that condition.
note: Ibn Atiyya favors the exception reading; al-Alusi says avoidance is the condition for expiating all interval sins.

view: Some legal theorists require repentance and nonpersistence in minor sins for expiation by good deeds; others dispute this requirement.
One claim says faith, the greatest good deed, removes unbelief and lesser sins, at least averting eternal punishment; Kharijites likewise argue two prayers can erase even omitted prayers.
Some hold that certain good deeds expiate even major sins; others object this makes repentance pointless, while al-Alusi replies that repentance remains obligatory even after expiation.
note: The disagreement is over scope of expiation and the independent duty to repent.

view: Sunni scholars allow punishment for minor sins despite avoiding major ones; Mu'tazilites deny it on their reading of 4:31.
Al-Ghazali says avoiding a major sin expiates only when one had desire and ability to commit it; al-Alusi interprets 4:31 as expiation at each time, not only after lifelong abstention.
When expiatory deeds meet major sins but no minor ones, al-Nawawi hopes they lighten the majors; Ibn Hajar's argument that avoiding major sins entails the five prayers is questioned.
Repentance from minor sins remains obligatory, with delay renewing sin; authorities dispute whether repentance for sins is certainly accepted or presumptive.
Another interpretation contrasts all good acts of the Prophet and believers with the evils of polytheists, promising victory and religious dominance; truth crushing falsehood is cited as a parallel.
The clause beginning 'indeed' explains and reinforces the command to pray by giving its reason: good deeds remove sins.

God-given good deeds erase faults inwardly: nearness, remorse, tears, repentance, forgiveness, divine solicitude, kindness, generosity, good opinion, favor, truthfulness, and sincerity remove different wrongs and spiritual defects.

The five senses veil the heart; prayer closes these distractions, opens it to divine light, and removes their darkness. Prayer at day edges preserves gathered presence, while night worship overcomes bodily dominance.
Knowledge of God, monotheism, struggle against the lower self, and remembrance purify the soul and heart, defeat Satan's schemes, and lift the luminous spirit from bodily darkness.
note: Bursevi compares nourishment of spirit to watering a seed that multiplies seven hundredfold.

view: Ablution symbolically washes away sins; one reported juristic consequence was treating the used ablution cloth as impure and disliking prayer in it.
A report says every drop of ablution water used by Ahmad's community earns a garden as broad as the sky.
Hafiz's Persian couplet praises prayer and supplication purified by tears and heart's blood.
The Prophet calls the profession 'There is no god but God' the best good deed; further reports promise it erases sins, with one chain judged weak and another unique.
'That' points to the immediately preceding command to establish prayer at these times, making prayer a setting for remembrance.
'That' points to the assertion that good deeds remove sins, encouraging people toward good actions.
'That' points to the foregoing commands and prohibitions, from steadfastness through prayer, or to the surah's counsel as a whole.
'That' refers to the Quran itself as a reminder.
'That' refers to what was just mentioned or to the promise itself.
The demonstrative dhālika is used in the sense of hādhā, 'this.'
Dhikrā means an admonition or, in another gloss, repentance.
Dhikrā is a verbal noun ending in feminine alif; discussions compare its pattern and plural with ʿadwā, daʿwā, and shūrā, and record the variant dhikr.
Those reminded are people who heed God's promise and warning, reflect, seek guidance, and benefit from admonition; sealed hearts do not respond.
Those who remember God in prosperity and adversity, hardship and ease, health and affliction receive the reminder; abundant remembrance also extends to standing, sitting, and lying down.
Prayer and expiation recall for spiritually attentive people clarity, gathered attention, intimacy, and spiritual taste.
The man in one occasion report kept remembering his offense afterward, explaining the phrase 'a reminder for those who remember.'
A man confessed forbidden kissing or intimacy short of intercourse; the verse was revealed or recited to him, and the Prophet said its guidance applies to everyone.
Some accounts specify that the man touched or struck the woman's backside; the Prophet delayed answering until the verse came.

The date seller Abu al-Yusr lured a woman into a house, embraced or kissed her, stopped short of intercourse, confessed after consulting Abu Bakr and Umar, and received the verse; the Prophet said his prayer expiated the act for everyone.
note: Variants say she was a date customer, the Prophet reproached betrayal of an absent fighter, and Gabriel brought the verse after Asr.

view: Accounts variously name the penitent Abu al-Yusr Ka'b ibn Amr, Abu Miqbal or Abu Nufayl Amir ibn Qays, Amr ibn Ghaziya, Abbad, or Ibn Muqib/Muattib.
note: The names differ across transmissions.

view: In some versions the man was told to perform careful ablution and pray, and the Prophet declared the remedy general to believers.
A man requested legal punishment for an offense; after ablution and prayer with the Prophet, he was told that God had cleansed him like a newborn.
A companion at a pool became aroused by a woman but stopped short of intercourse; he repented, and the Prophet told him to seek forgiveness and pray four units before citing the verse.
Another occasion report involves a flour seller who kissed a woman and sought counsel from Abu Bakr, Umar, and the Prophet; Ata interprets the commanded prayers as obligatory.
Reports differ on who asked whether the verse was specific to the penitent: Umar, Muadh, or Abu al-Yusr.

The main Ibn Masud incident report is graded hasan sahih by Tirmidhi; his Abu al-Yusr report is called hasan gharib with a weakened transmitter, and other Muadh and Abu al-Yusr routes are called weak.
Some reports say the verse was already revealed and was applied to the penitent, whereas others describe its fresh revelation.

The incident supports the ruling that forbidden kissing or touching short of intercourse incurs no fixed penalty; Ibn al-Mundhir extends this to no discretionary penalty for a man and woman found in one garment.

Some regard this verse as a Medinan exception within a Meccan surah, citing the report that it was revealed to the penitent; others regard the entire surah as Meccan and take 'revealed' as application.

The verse may precede the Night Journey's five-prayer obligation: two daily prayers and night vigil were initially prescribed, then the vigil was abrogated for the community and perhaps later for the Prophet.
If the verse was revealed later, its placement fits the preceding command to be upright and the following command to be patient.
Ali reports that the prayer command is the Quran's most hopeful verse; in a dialogue he rejects other suggested forgiveness verses before citing it.
Al-Sadiq urges daily self-accounting because angels record hidden and public deeds; neither small sins nor good deeds should be dismissed, for a good deed may erase an old grave sin.
An austere worshiper who made others despair of God's mercy was himself made to despair after death; a mother bird's concern for its chick illustrates God's still greater mercy to believers.
A report says God distributes worldly provision broadly but gives faith to those He loves; it links faith to a surrendered heart and tongue and neighbors safe from harm.
The verse's prayer interpretations resemble disputes over the middlemost prayer at 2:238.
The Quranic declaration of religion's completion confirms that prophetic explanation supplied everything needed for prayer.
One report locates the revelation of the good-deeds clause in the case of Nabhan the date seller.
In Ibn Masud's account, the man had intimate contact with a woman near Medina; Umar advised that since God had concealed his sin, he should have concealed it too.
God covers a believer's sin, forgives it, and then replaces it with good deeds, as in 25:70.
In one confession report, the touched woman's husband was away on campaign; Umar said the newly revealed prayer remedy applies to all believers, and the Prophet agreed.
The reminder strengthens believers in their religion.
In Burayda's date-seller report, the Prophet prayed with the penitent, explained the five prayers named by the verse, and said their cleansing benefit applies to everyone.
Al-Dahhak is reported to accept all three explanations of the second day end: Maghrib, Asr alone, or Zuhr and Asr.
